text: It is the eighteenth of July.
Priya has three days to file her fund's quarterly return.
She opens the administrator's statement. Drawn capital: seventeen point eight million.
She opens her own ledger. Nineteen point three.
Both official. Both signed. Neither is wrong.
She cannot tell an error from a timing difference.
So she emails the administrator.
The answer comes back in a reply, and that reply is now the only record of why she filed what she filed.
She signs personally.
In October, Priya leaves.
Her successor opens the same fund, finds the same two numbers, and none of the reasoning.
The records must survive eight years. The reasoning survives fifteen days.
Every system built for this picks one.
Take the figure most documents agree on. It files seventeen point eight.
That is the wrong number, and nothing announces it.
We refuse to pick.
Every number is pinned to the exact line it came from, and the moment it was true.
Both documents are correct.
A capital call landed at five forty-two in the evening, after the administrator had closed at four.
And this number appears in no document at all.
So it cannot be decided. Only attested, by a named person.
Nine roles. Forty steps.
Half of them contain no model at all, because a model cannot check a model.
Priya decides, in writing. Rajiv confirms.
Then it seals, and one changed byte breaks the chain.
Twenty-four out of twenty-four planted failures, caught.
Zero silent picks. A full case in under eight seconds.
Every document here is fictional. We have never seen a real quarterly return.
But when Priya's successor opens that fund, she reads why.
